cmp.en: Addhagū, "one who travels the long road," means one wandering in the round of rebirth. The plain Chinese 在生死路上奔走的人 ("one running on the road of birth and death") supplies "birth and death"; the English "wanderer" stays literal.

verses.en: One who has faith, is complete in virtue, and is blessed with good name and wealth is honored wherever he goes.
The good shine from afar, like the Himalaya mountains; the bad are not seen even when near, like arrows shot in the night.
Sitting alone, sleeping alone, walking alone without slacking, alone taming himself, he should find delight at the forest's edge.
The one who says what did not happen goes to hell, and so does the one who, having done something, says, "I didn't do it." Both become alike after death, people of base deeds in the world beyond.
Many with the ochre robe around their necks are of evil character and unrestrained. These evildoers, by their evil deeds, are reborn in hell.
Better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, burning like a flame, than for one without virtue and restraint to eat the alms of the country.

cmp.note: raṭṭha-piṇḍa「国家的食团」，指百姓供养给出家人的饭。白话「全国百姓供养的饭」、英文 the alms of the country 都补出了「供养」。
cmp.en: Raṭṭha-piṇḍa, "the country's alms-food," is the food lay people give to renunciants. The plain Chinese 全国百姓供养的饭 ("food offered by the people of the whole country") and the English "the alms of the country" both make the giving explicit.

verses.en: Four things befall the careless man who goes after another's wife: a gain of demerit, an uneasy sleep, blame as the third, and hell as the fourth.

cmp.note: a-puñña-lābha「得到非福」，就是造下了恶业。白话写「得到恶报」，把「造业」说成了「受报」；英文 a gain of demerit 照字面。
cmp.en: A-puñña-lābha, "a gain of demerit," means making bad kamma. The plain Chinese 得到恶报 ("receiving evil retribution") turns making kamma into receiving its result; the English "a gain of demerit" stays literal.

verses.en: A gain of demerit and a bad destination; the brief pleasure of a frightened man with a frightened woman; and the king imposes a heavy punishment. So a man should not go after another's wife.
As kusa grass wrongly grasped cuts the hand, so the renunciant's life wrongly handled drags one down to hell.
Any slack action, any corrupted vow, a holy life lived under suspicion: none of these brings great fruit.
If something is to be done, do it; take it on firmly. A slack wanderer only scatters more dust.
A bad deed is better left undone, for a bad deed torments you afterwards; a good deed is better done, for having done it you have no regret.
Like a frontier city guarded inside and out, so guard yourselves. Do not let the moment pass you by; those who let the moment pass grieve when they are consigned to hell.

cmp.note: khaṇa「时机」，注释家解作「生而为人、遇到佛法」这个难得的时机。白话「时机」、英文 the moment 都照字面。
cmp.en: Khaṇa, "the moment, the opportunity," is explained by the commentators as the rare chance of being born human and meeting the Dhamma. The plain Chinese 时机 (shíjī) and the English "the moment" stay literal.

verses.en: Ashamed of what is not shameful, unashamed of what is shameful, holding wrong views, beings go to a bad destination.
Seeing danger where there is none and no danger where there is danger, holding wrong views, beings go to a bad destination.
Seeing fault where there is none and no fault where there is fault, holding wrong views, beings go to a bad destination.
Knowing fault as fault and the faultless as faultless, holding right views, beings go to a good destination.
As an elephant in battle endures the arrow shot from the bow, so I will endure abuse; for most people are of poor conduct.

cmp.note: nāga 可以是「大象」，也可以是「龙、蛇」，还可以比喻「圣者、大人物」。这一品的 nāga 都是大象，但也暗含「圣者」的意思。白话「大象」、英文 elephant 只能取一层。
cmp.en: Nāga can mean "elephant," "serpent, dragon," or figuratively "a great one, a sage." In this chapter it is the elephant, with the sense of "great one" in the background. The plain Chinese 大象 (dàxiàng, "elephant") and the English "elephant" can take only one layer.

verses.en: They lead the tamed one into a crowd; the king mounts the tamed one. Best among people is the tamed one who endures abuse.
Excellent are tamed mules, thoroughbred horses from the Sindhu, and great tusked elephants; but one who has tamed himself is better still.
For not by these mounts can one go to the land never gone to, as the tamed one goes by his own well-tamed self.
The elephant called Dhanapāla ("Guardian of Wealth"), in fierce rut and hard to hold back, eats not a mouthful when bound: the elephant longs for the elephant forest.
When someone is sluggish and a glutton, a sleeper who rolls about as he lies, like a great hog fattened on fodder, that dullard goes into the womb again and again.
This mind used to wander wherever it wished, wherever it liked, as it pleased. Today I will hold it in check wisely, as the trainer with his hook holds an elephant in rut.
Delight in heedfulness, guard your own minds. Pull yourselves out of the hard place, like an elephant sunk in the mud.
If you find a wise companion to walk with you, of good conduct and steady, overcoming all dangers, walk with him gladly and mindfully.
If you do not find a wise companion to walk with you, of good conduct and steady, then, like a king who has left a conquered kingdom, walk alone, like an elephant in the elephant forest.
Better to walk alone; there is no companionship with a fool. Walk alone and do no evil, at ease, like an elephant in the elephant forest.
Friends are a joy when need arises; contentment with whatever there is is a joy; merit is a joy at the end of life; the abandoning of all suffering is a joy.
A joy in the world is caring for one's mother, and a joy is caring for one's father; a joy in the world is honoring renunciants, and a joy is honoring brahmins.

cmp.note: matteyyatā 可以是「孝敬母亲」，也可以是「慈母般的心」；sāmaññatā、brahmaññatā 可以是「敬重沙门、婆罗门」，也可以是「做沙门、做婆罗门（的品格）」。白话和英文都取注释家的「孝敬、敬重」读法。
cmp.en: Matteyyatā can mean "caring for one's mother" or "being motherly"; sāmaññatā and brahmaññatā can mean "honoring renunciants and brahmins" or "the character of a renunciant, of a brahmin." The plain Chinese and the English both follow the commentarial reading of "caring for, honoring."

verses.en: A joy is virtue lasting into old age; a joy is faith firmly planted; a joy is the gaining of wisdom; a joy is not doing evil.
For a person who lives carelessly, craving grows like a māluvā creeper. He leaps from life to life, like a monkey in the forest looking for fruit.

cmp.note: taṇhā 字面是「口渴」。白话「渴爱」、英文 craving 都保留了停不下来的饥渴。
cmp.en: Taṇhā literally means "thirst." The plain Chinese 渴爱 (kě'ài, "thirsting love") and the English "craving" both keep the restless hunger.

cmp.note: hurā huraṁ「从这里到那里」，注释家解作从一世到另一世。白话、英文都取了这个解释。
cmp.en: Hurā huraṁ, "from here to there," is explained by the commentators as from one life to the next. The plain Chinese and the English both take that reading.

verses.en: Whoever is overcome by this wretched craving, this clinging in the world, his sorrows grow like bīraṇa grass after rain.
But whoever overcomes this wretched craving, so hard to get past in the world, his sorrows fall away from him like drops of water from a lotus leaf.

So I say to you, all who are gathered here, good fortune to you: dig up the root of craving, as one who wants the fragrant root digs up bīraṇa grass. Do not let Māra break you again and again, as a stream breaks a reed.

cmp.note: usīra 是毗罗那草（bīraṇa）的香根，可以做香料。白话「要香根的人」、英文 one who wants the fragrant root 都补出了「香根」。
cmp.en: Usīra is the fragrant root of bīraṇa grass, used for perfume. The plain Chinese 要香根的人 ("one who wants the fragrant root") and the English both supply "fragrant root."

verses.en: As a tree, though cut down, grows again if its roots are unharmed and firm, so while the underlying tendency to craving is not rooted out, this suffering arises again and again.

cmp.note: anusaya「随眠、潜在倾向」：平时睡着、条件一到就醒来的烦恼。白话「潜伏的习性」、英文 underlying tendency 都译出了。
cmp.en: Anusaya, "latent tendency": a defilement that lies dormant and wakes when conditions arise. The plain Chinese 潜伏的习性 ("lurking habit") and the English "underlying tendency" both convey it.

verses.en: One in whom the thirty-six streams rushing toward the pleasant are strong: his thoughts bound up with passion sweep away that person of wrong view.

cmp.note: 「三十六条水流」，注释家解作十八种渴爱（对六根、六境、六识）乘以内外两种。白话、英文都照字面，没有展开。
cmp.en: "Thirty-six streams": the commentators explain them as eighteen kinds of craving (for the six senses, six objects and six consciousnesses), times two, internal and external. The plain Chinese and the English stay literal without unpacking it.

verses.en: The streams flow everywhere; the creeper sprouts and takes hold. Seeing that the creeper has grown, cut its root with wisdom.
A person's pleasures are flowing and oiled with affection. Bound to what is agreeable, seeking happiness, such people are subject to birth and old age.
Driven by craving, people run about like a snared hare. Caught in fetters and attachments, they come to suffering again and again, for a long time.
Driven by craving, people run about like a snared hare. Therefore one who longs for his own freedom from passion should drive out craving.

cmp.note: 本站底本这一句没有 bhikkhu「比丘」，白话加了「比丘」；别的版本有作 bhikkhu ākaṅkhī virāgam attano 的。英文照底本写 one who longs。
cmp.en: This edition has no bhikkhu in this line, yet the plain Chinese adds 比丘 (bǐqiū, "monk"); some other editions read bhikkhu ākaṅkhī virāgam attano. The English follows this edition with "one who longs."

verses.en: One who has left the forest but is drawn to the forest, freed from the forest, runs right back to the forest: come, look at that person, freed, he runs right back into bondage.

cmp.note: 又是 vana「树林／欲望」的双关（见第 283 偈）：离开了欲望的林子，心又倾向欲望，跑回去。这一偈注释家讲的是一位还俗的比丘。白话「心倾向林外的自由」和原文不太合：vanādhimutto 是「倾心于林子」。英文 drawn to the forest 照原文。
cmp.en: Another pun on vana, "forest / desire" (see verse 283): having left the forest of desire, the mind leans back toward it and runs back. The commentarial story is about a monk who returned to lay life. The plain Chinese 心倾向林外的自由 ("the mind inclines to freedom outside the forest") doesn't quite fit: vanādhimutto means "drawn to the forest." The English "drawn to the forest" follows the Pali.

verses.en: The wise do not call that a strong bond which is made of iron, wood or rope; but infatuation with jewels and earrings, and longing for children and wives:
that, say the wise, is the strong bond, dragging down, loose-seeming, hard to undo. Cutting even this, they go forth, free of longing, having left sensual pleasure behind.
Those dyed with passion fall back into the stream they themselves made, as a spider into its own web. Cutting even this, the wise go on, free of longing, having left all suffering behind.
Let go of the past, let go of the future, let go of the present, gone beyond existence. With your mind released in every way, you will not come again to birth and old age.

cmp.note: 「前、后、中」，注释家解作过去、未来、现在。白话照字面写「前面、后面、中间」，英文直接写 past / future / present。
cmp.en: "In front, behind, in the middle" is explained by the commentators as past, future and present. The plain Chinese keeps the literal 前面、后面、中间 ("in front, behind, in between"); the English says "past / future / present" directly.

verses.en: For a person churned by thoughts, of strong passion, looking at what is attractive, craving grows all the more: he is making his bond stronger.
But one who delights in calming thoughts, who always mindfully develops the perception of the unattractive, he will make an end of craving, he will cut Māra's bond.

cmp.note: asubha「不美」：观察身体并不美好，用来对治贪恋（参见《大念处经》观身的部分）。白话括号里说明了；英文 the perception of the unattractive 照字面。
cmp.en: Asubha, "the unattractive": contemplating the body as not beautiful, as an antidote to lust (see the body contemplations in the Great Discourse on Mindfulness). The plain Chinese explains it in brackets; the English "the perception of the unattractive" is literal.

verses.en: He has reached the goal, fearless, free of craving, without blemish; he has cut out the darts of existence. This is his last body.

Free of craving, without grasping, skilled in words and their meanings, knowing how letters combine and which comes before and after: he is called "one in his last body, of great wisdom, a great person."

cmp.note: 「通晓词句和语言」：注释家解作通达四无碍解（义、法、词、辩）。这一偈把阿罗汉描写成精通语言的人，有点出人意料。白话、英文都照字面。
cmp.en: "Skilled in words and their meanings": the commentators explain it as mastery of the four analytical knowledges (of meaning, of teaching, of language, of eloquence). Describing an arahant as an expert in language is a little surprising. The plain Chinese and the English both stay literal.

verses.en: "I have overcome all, I know all, I am untainted by all things. I have let go of all, freed in the ending of craving. Having understood by myself, whom should I point to as my teacher?"

cmp.note: 传统说这是佛陀觉悟后对外道 Upaka 说的话：他的觉悟没有老师。白话、英文都照字面，没有补出这个背景。
cmp.en: Tradition says the Buddha spoke this after his awakening to the wandering ascetic Upaka: his awakening had no teacher. The plain Chinese and the English stay literal without adding this background.

verses.en: The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes; delight in the Dhamma surpasses all delights; the ending of craving overcomes all suffering.
Wealth destroys the foolish, but not those who seek the far shore. Through craving for wealth the fool destroys himself as he would destroy others.
Fields are spoiled by weeds; people are spoiled by passion. So what is given to those free of passion bears great fruit.
Fields are spoiled by weeds; people are spoiled by hatred. So what is given to those free of hatred bears great fruit.
Fields are spoiled by weeds; people are spoiled by delusion. So what is given to those free of delusion bears great fruit.
Fields are spoiled by weeds; people are spoiled by wanting. So what is given to those free of wanting bears great fruit.
Restraint of the eye is good, good is restraint of the ear; restraint of the nose is good, good is restraint of the tongue.
Restraint of the body is good, good is restraint of speech; restraint of the mind is good, good is restraint everywhere. The bhikkhu restrained everywhere is freed from all suffering.
Controlled in hand, controlled in foot, controlled in speech, controlled in the highest, delighting within, composed, alone and content: him they call a bhikkhu.

cmp.note: saṁyat-uttama 可以读成「在最高处（头）受控制的」，也可以读成「最受控制的」。白话取前一种并补了「头脑」；英文 controlled in the highest 照字面保留两可。
cmp.en: Saṁyat-uttama can be read as "controlled in the highest part (the head)" or as "supremely controlled." The plain Chinese takes the first and adds 头脑 ("the head"); the English "controlled in the highest" keeps both readings open.

verses.en: The bhikkhu who controls his mouth, who speaks wisely and is not puffed up, who explains the meaning and the Dhamma: sweet are his words.
Dwelling in the Dhamma, delighting in the Dhamma, reflecting on the Dhamma, recollecting the Dhamma, a bhikkhu does not fall away from the true Dhamma.
Do not look down on what you have received, and do not live envying others. A bhikkhu who envies others does not attain concentration.
Though a bhikkhu receives little, if he does not look down on what he receives, the gods praise him, pure in livelihood and not lazy.
One who has no sense of "mine" toward name-and-form in any way, and does not grieve for what is not: he is truly called a bhikkhu.

cmp.note: asatā 可以读成「因为（它）不存在了」，也可以读成「对不存在的东西」。白话「失去了也不忧愁」意译；英文 does not grieve for what is not 照字面。
cmp.en: Asatā can be read as "because it no longer exists" or "over what does not exist." The plain Chinese 失去了也不忧愁 ("not grieving when it is lost") paraphrases; the English "does not grieve for what is not" stays literal.

verses.en: The bhikkhu who dwells in loving-kindness, with clear confidence in the Buddha's teaching, will reach the peaceful state, the happiness of the stilling of conditioned things.

cmp.note: mettā「慈」来自 mitta「朋友」，是朋友般的善意。白话「慈心」、英文 loving-kindness 都是约定俗成的译法（参见《慈经》）。
cmp.en: Mettā comes from mitta, "friend": the goodwill of a friend. The plain Chinese 慈心 (cíxīn) and the English "loving-kindness" are the conventional renderings (see the Discourse on Loving-kindness).

verses.en: Bail out this boat, bhikkhu; once bailed, it will go lightly for you. Having cut off passion and hatred, you will reach nibbāna.
Cut off five, give up five, and develop five more. The bhikkhu who has gone beyond five attachments is called "one who has crossed the flood."

cmp.note: 这一偈是个数字谜：注释家说，要斩断的五样是五下分结，要舍弃的五样是五上分结，要修习的五样是信、精进、念、定、慧五根，五种执著是贪、瞋、痴、慢、见。白话、英文都照字面，答案写在注里。
cmp.en: This verse is a number puzzle. According to the commentators, the five to cut off are the five lower fetters, the five to give up are the five higher fetters, the five to develop are the five faculties (faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom), and the five attachments are greed, hatred, delusion, conceit and views. The plain Chinese and the English stay literal; the answers are given here.

verses.en: Meditate, bhikkhu, do not be careless; do not let your mind whirl in sensual pleasures. Do not carelessly swallow the iron ball, and cry, as you burn, "This is suffering!"
There is no meditation for one without wisdom, no wisdom for one who does not meditate. One who has both meditation and wisdom is close to nibbāna.

cmp.note: jhāna 是深度专注的心境，中文译「禅定」，英文这里写 meditation，是为了读起来顺；更准确的是「禅那、入定」。
cmp.en: Jhāna is a state of deep absorption, rendered 禅定 (chándìng) in Chinese. The English uses "meditation" here for readability; more precisely it is meditative absorption.

verses.en: For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, his mind at peace, seeing the Dhamma rightly, there is a joy beyond the human.
Whenever he reflects on the rising and passing away of the aggregates, he gains joy and gladness: for those who understand, that is the deathless.
For a wise bhikkhu, this is the beginning here: guarding the senses, contentment, and restraint according to the Pātimokkha (the core monastic code).
Keep company with good friends, pure in livelihood and not lazy. Be friendly in your ways, skilled in conduct; then, full of gladness, you will make an end of suffering.
As the jasmine sheds its withered flowers, so, bhikkhus, should you shed passion and hatred.
Calm in body, calm in speech, calm and well composed, the bhikkhu who has spat out the bait of the world is called "one at peace."

cmp.note: āmisa「诱饵、肉」，世间的诱饵就是欲乐和名利。白话「世间的诱饵」、英文 the bait of the world 都保留了这个画面（参见《大念处经》观受部分）。
cmp.en: Āmisa means "bait, flesh"; the bait of the world is sensual pleasure, fame and gain. The plain Chinese 世间的诱饵 ("the world's bait") and the English "the bait of the world" both keep the image (see the contemplation of feelings in the Great Discourse on Mindfulness).

verses.en: Urge yourself on by yourself, examine yourself by yourself. Self-guarded and mindful, bhikkhu, you will live happily.
You are your own refuge; who else could be your refuge? You are your own destination. So restrain yourself, as a merchant trains a fine horse.
The bhikkhu full of gladness, with clear confidence in the Buddha's teaching, will reach the peaceful state, the happiness of the stilling of conditioned things.
The bhikkhu who, though young, devotes himself to the Buddha's teaching lights up this world, like the moon set free from a cloud.
Cut the stream with effort, drive out sensual desires, brahmin! Knowing the ending of conditioned things, you are one who knows the unmade, brahmin.

cmp.note: brāhmaṇa 本是古印度的祭司种姓，生来就是。这一品里佛陀把这个词拿过来，重新定义成「真正清净的人」，跟出身无关。白话在括号里说明了；英文保留 brahmin，第 393 偈正面说出这层意思。
cmp.en: Brāhmaṇa originally means a member of the hereditary priestly caste of ancient India. In this chapter the Buddha takes the word over and redefines it as "one who is truly pure," regardless of birth. The plain Chinese explains this in brackets; the English keeps "brahmin," and verse 393 states the point directly.

cmp.note: akataññū 字面可以是「忘恩的」，这里是「知道非造作（涅槃）的」，跟第 97 偈同一个双关。
cmp.en: Akataññū can mean "ungrateful," but here it means "knowing the unmade (nibbāna)," the same pun as in verse 97.

verses.en: When the brahmin has gone beyond in two things, all the bonds of that knowing one come to an end.

cmp.note: 「两种法」，注释家解作止（samatha）和观（vipassanā）。白话、英文都照字面，没有展开。
cmp.en: "Two things" is explained by the commentators as calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). The plain Chinese and the English both stay literal without unpacking it.

verses.en: For whom there is neither this shore nor the far shore nor both, who is free of distress and unbound: him I call a brahmin.
One who meditates, free of dust, settled, his task done, without taints, who has reached the highest goal: him I call a brahmin.
The sun shines by day, the moon glows by night, the warrior shines in his armor, the brahmin shines in meditation; but all day and all night the Buddha shines in his splendor.

cmp.note: tapati「发热、发光」，跟 tapa「苦行」同根。白话「发光、闪耀」、英文 shines 都只取了光。
cmp.en: Tapati means "to glow, to burn," from the same root as tapa, "austerity." The plain Chinese 发光、闪耀 ("give off light, shine") and the English "shines" take only the light.

verses.en: Because he has put away evil he is called a brahmin; because he lives in calm he is called a renunciant; because he drives out his own stains he is called one who has gone forth.

cmp.note: 三个都是文字游戏：brāhmaṇa 被解作 bāhita-pāpa「排除了恶的」，samaṇa 被解作 sama-cariyā「平和地行」，pabbajita「出家人」被解作 pabbājeti「赶走（污垢）」。白话、英文都只能译出意思。
cmp.en: All three are wordplay: brāhmaṇa is glossed as bāhita-pāpa, "one who has put away evil"; samaṇa as sama-cariyā, "living in calm"; pabbajita, "one who has gone forth," as pabbājeti, "drives out" (stains). The plain Chinese and the English can give only the meaning.

verses.en: Do not strike a brahmin, and let no brahmin unleash his anger on the one who strikes him. Shame on the one who strikes a brahmin; greater shame on the one who unleashes his anger.
Nothing is better for a brahmin than this: holding the mind back from what is dear. Wherever the wish to harm turns away, there suffering is stilled.
One who does no wrong by body, speech or mind, restrained in these three: him I call a brahmin.
From whomever one learns the Dhamma taught by the Fully Awakened One, one should honor him with care, as a brahmin honors the sacrificial fire.
Not by matted hair, not by clan, not by birth does one become a brahmin. In whom there is truth and Dhamma, he is pure, he is a brahmin.

cmp.note: jacca「出身」：这一偈正面否定了「婆罗门是生来的」。白话、英文都照字面。古印度的种姓制度是这一品的背景。
cmp.en: Jacca means "birth": this verse directly rejects the idea that one is a brahmin by birth. The plain Chinese and the English both translate literally; the caste system of ancient India is the background of the whole chapter.

verses.en: What use is your matted hair, fool? What use your antelope-skin robe? Inside you is a thicket, and you polish the outside.
One who wears rag-robes, lean, his veins standing out, meditating alone in the forest: him I call a brahmin.

cmp.note: paṁsu-kūla 字面是「垃圾堆」，指从垃圾堆、坟场捡来的破布缝成的衣。白话把来历说清楚了；英文 rag-robes 只说了「破布衣」。
cmp.en: Paṁsu-kūla literally means "rubbish heap": robes sewn from rags picked up from rubbish heaps and charnel grounds. The plain Chinese spells out where the cloth comes from; the English "rag-robes" says only that they are rags.

verses.en: I do not call him a brahmin who is born of a womb, sprung from a mother. If he still owns things, he is just a "bho-sayer" (one who addresses others haughtily). One who owns nothing and grasps at nothing: him I call a brahmin.

cmp.note: bho 是婆罗门对别人说话时的称呼，带一点居高临下，像「喂」。bhovādī「说 bho 的人」是在挖苦只有身份、没有德行的婆罗门。白话照字面译成「称呼别人『喂』的人」，英文保留原词并加括号说明。
cmp.en: Bho is how brahmins addressed others, a little condescending, like "hey, you." Bhovādī, "a bho-sayer," mocks brahmins who have the status but not the virtue. The plain Chinese renders it literally as 称呼别人「喂」的人 ("one who calls others 'hey'"); the English keeps the word and explains it in brackets.

verses.en: One who has cut every fetter, who does not tremble, who has gone beyond ties and is unbound: him I call a brahmin.
One who has cut the strap and the thong, the chain together with its fittings, who has lifted the bar, the awakened one: him I call a brahmin.

cmp.note: 这一串都是比喻，注释家解作：皮带是瞋恨，绳索是渴爱，链子是六十二种邪见，缰绳是潜在倾向，门闩是无明。白话、英文都照字面。
cmp.en: These are all images, explained by the commentators as: the strap is hatred, the thong craving, the chain the sixty-two wrong views, its fittings the latent tendencies, and the bar ignorance. The plain Chinese and the English stay literal.

verses.en: One who without anger endures abuse, beating and bonds, whose army is the power of patience: him I call a brahmin.
One who is free of anger, devout, virtuous, not swollen with pride, tamed, in his last body: him I call a brahmin.
Like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle, one who does not cling to sensual pleasures: him I call a brahmin.
One who knows, right here, the ending of his own suffering, who has laid down the burden and is unbound: him I call a brahmin.
One of deep wisdom, intelligent, who knows the path from what is not the path, who has reached the highest goal: him I call a brahmin.
One who does not mix with householders or with the homeless, who wanders without a home and wants little: him I call a brahmin.
One who has laid down the rod toward all beings, the trembling and the firm, who neither kills nor causes killing: him I call a brahmin.
Unhostile among the hostile, at peace among those who take up the rod, not grasping among those who grasp: him I call a brahmin.
One from whom passion and hatred, pride and contempt have fallen away like a mustard seed from the point of a needle: him I call a brahmin.
One who speaks words that are not harsh, that inform, that are true, by which he offends no one: him I call a brahmin.
One who here in the world takes nothing not given, long or short, small or large, fine or poor: him I call a brahmin.
One who has no longings for this world or the next, without longing and unbound: him I call a brahmin.
One who has no attachments, who through understanding is free of doubt, who has plunged into the deathless: him I call a brahmin.
One who here has gone beyond the tie to both merit and evil, sorrowless, dustless, pure: him I call a brahmin.
One who is like the moon, spotless and pure, clear and unclouded, in whom delight in existence is destroyed: him I call a brahmin.

One who has passed beyond this swampy road, this hard path, the round of rebirth and delusion, who has crossed and reached the far shore, meditative, unmoved, free of doubt, at peace through not clinging: him I call a brahmin.
One who here has given up sensual pleasures and wanders homeless, in whom sensual desire and existence are destroyed: him I call a brahmin.
One who here has given up craving and wanders homeless, in whom craving and existence are destroyed: him I call a brahmin.

cmp.note: 本站底本这一段把整首偈抄了两遍，应是录文重复；白话只译一遍，英文也只译一遍。
cmp.en: This edition copies the whole verse twice, apparently a duplication in the transcription; the plain Chinese translates it once, and so does the English.

verses.en: One who has left behind the human bond and gone beyond the divine bond, released from all bonds: him I call a brahmin.
One who has left behind delight and discontent, who has become cool, without a basis for rebirth, a hero who has conquered the whole world: him I call a brahmin.

cmp.note: sīti-bhūta「变得清凉」：烦恼是火，熄了就凉，跟 nibbāna「熄灭」呼应。白话「清凉」、英文 cool 都保留了这个意思。
cmp.en: Sīti-bhūta, "become cool": the defilements are fire, and when it goes out one is cool, echoing nibbāna, "going out." The plain Chinese 清凉 (qīngliáng) and the English "cool" both keep this.

verses.en: One who knows fully the passing away and rebirth of beings, unattached, well gone, awakened: him I call a brahmin.
One whose destination gods, gandhabbas and humans do not know, whose taints are destroyed, an arahant: him I call a brahmin.
One who has nothing before, behind or in between, who owns nothing and grasps at nothing: him I call a brahmin.
The bull, the noble one, the hero, the great seer, the victor, unmoved, washed clean, awakened: him I call a brahmin.

cmp.note: nhātaka「沐浴过的人」，在婆罗门传统里指学成出师、行过沐浴礼的人；佛陀把它解作洗净了烦恼的人。白话「已洗净」、英文 washed clean 都照字面。
cmp.en: Nhātaka, "one who has bathed," in brahmin tradition means a student who has finished his studies and taken the ritual bath; the Buddha reinterprets it as one washed clean of defilements. The plain Chinese 已洗净 (yǐ xǐjìng, "already washed clean") and the English "washed clean" are literal.

verses.en: One who knows his former lives, who sees heaven and the states of woe, who has reached the end of birth, a sage perfected in direct knowledge, who has completed all that is to be completed: him I call a brahmin.
